title: Why civilizations are not states
summary: A political map shows where sovereignty ends. It cannot, on its own, show where a civilization continues. Languages, religions and trading networks may cross several states with clearly drawn borders. Treating a civilization as a colored territory confuses political unity with the whole of cultural, intellectual and social life.

blocks.text: A political map shows where sovereignty ends. It cannot, on its own, show where a civilization continues. Languages, religions and trading networks may cross several states with clearly drawn borders. Treating a civilization as a colored territory confuses political unity with the whole of cultural, intellectual and social life.

Sumerian cities competed with one another, and Greek city-states did not maintain a single enduring political center. Yet they could share writing, beliefs and spaces of exchange. Indian Ocean ports remained connected through monsoons, merchants and religion without first becoming one empire. Civilizational connections could extend well beyond political control.

Observation therefore begins with choosing a unit. Everyday cooperation in a village, exchange among strangers in a city, state taxation and law, and continuity across regions answer different questions. Nor can records from an imperial center automatically represent the experiences of villages, frontiers and mobile populations.

Civilizational boundaries are overlapping layers. Politics, language, knowledge, belief and commerce may each draw a different boundary. These boundaries preserve continuity while allowing exchange. This helps explain why political fragmentation need not end a civilization, and why stronger connections need not make societies identical.
